query: For quantifying a minor element at 0.2-0.5 wt% (e.g. Mg in an Al-10Si-0.4Mg alloy, AlSi10Mg) by SEM-EDS, is a matrix-matched standard whose bulk composition was certified by ICP-MS preferable to pure-element standards? How large are matrix (ZAF) correction and standardless-quantification errors at such concentrations, and what accuracy and detection limits can standards-based EDS achieve for minor/trace elements?

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan for to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string representing the plan. It should be a dictionary
with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child
        - ADULT: Adult
        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting
        - SUSPENDED: Study suspended
        - TERMINATED: Study terminated
        - WITHDRAWN: Study withdrawn
        - AVAILABLE: Available
        - NO_LONGER_AVAILABLE: No longer available
        - TEMPORARILY_NOT_AVAILABLE: Temporarily not available
        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training
        - SUPPORTIVE_CARE: Supportive Care
        - SCREENING: Screening
        - HEALTH_SERVICES_RESEARCH: Health Services Research
        - BASIC_SCIENCE: Basic Science

    InterventionType:
        - BEHAVIORAL: Behavioral interventions

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.
answer.title: Answer

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: For quantifying a minor element at 0.2-0.5 wt% (e.g. Mg in an Al-10Si-0.4Mg alloy, AlSi10Mg) by SEM-EDS, is a matrix-matched standard whose bulk composition was certified by ICP-MS preferable to pure-element standards? How large are matrix (ZAF) correction and standardless-quantification errors at such concentrations, and what accuracy and detection limits can standards-based EDS achieve for minor/trace elements?

Abstract:
Abstract 2018 marked the 50th anniversary of the introduction of energy dispersive X-ray spectrometry (EDS) with semiconductor detectors to electron-excited X-ray microanalysis. Initially useful for qualitative analysis, EDS has developed into a fully quantitative analytical tool that can match wavelength dispersive spectrometry for accuracy in the determination of major (mass concentration C > 0.1) and minor (0.01 ≤ C ≤ 0.1) constituents, and useful accuracy can extend well into the trace (0.001 < C < 0.01) constituent range even when severe peak interference occurs. Accurate analysis is possible for low atomic number elements (B, C, N, O, and F), and at low beam energy, which can optimize lateral and depth spatial resolution. By recording a full EDS spectrum at each picture element of a scan, comprehensive quantitative compositional mapping can also be performed.

Abstract:
It is a great time to be a microanalyst. After a few decades of incremental progress in energy-dispersive X-ray spectrometry (EDS), the last decade has seen the accuracy and precision surge forward. Today, the question is not whether EDS is generally useful but to identify the types of problems for which wavelength-dispersive X-ray spectrometry remains the better choice. The full extent of EDS’s capabilities has surprised many. Low Z, low energy, and trace element detection have been demonstrated even in the presence of extreme peak interferences. In this paper, we will summarise the state-of-the-art and investigate a challenging problem domain, the analysis of minerals bearing multiple rare-earth elements.

An electron microprobe is an electron microscope designed for the non-destructive x-ray microanalysis and imaging of solid materials. It is essentially a hybrid instrument combining the capabilities of both the scanning electron microscope (SEM) and an x-ray fluorescence spectrometer (XRF), with the added features of fine-spot focusing (~ 1 micrometer), optical microscope imaging, and precision-automated sample positioning. The analyst makes measurements while observing the sample (with the optical microscope or with a secondary/backscattered electron image) and selecting specific analysis locations (using the precision sample stage).

We report a simple, scalable route to produce ultrahigh-strength magnesium (Mg) via solidification of a colloidal solution containing nanoscale niobium carbide (NbC) particles suspended in liquid magnesium (Mg(l)). A single-atom-level investigation reveals that NbC exhibits excellent spontaneous wetting with molten Mg, driven by the formation of an ordered layer of Mg atoms strongly bonded to the carbon atoms on the NbC {001} surface. This creates a novel type of Mg-coated NbC (Mg@NbC) particles in liquid Mg and is referred to as Mg(l)-Mg@NbC nanocolloid. This unique and spontaneous wetting behaviour enables uniform nanoparticle dispersion in the molten Mg without external fields, and in the solidified Mg matrix without the need for thermomechanical processing. ## 1. Quantitative SEM/EDS, Step 1: What Constitutes a Sufficiently Flat Specimen?

Relevant Snippet:
The most rigorous quantitative electron-excited x-ray microanalysis that can be performed with scanning electron microscopy/energy dispersive x-ray spectrometry (SEM/EDS) follows the k ratio protocol: measure the x-ray intensity ratio k= Iunknown/Istandard for each element and calculate concentrations by applying matrix corrections for electron backscattering and energy loss (Z), x-ray absorption (A), and characteristic-and continuum-induced secondary x-ray fluorescence (F), as originally developed for the electron probe microanalyzer (EPMA) with wavelength dispersive spectrometry (WDS)[1]. By utilizing the k ratio protocol, SEM/EDS has been shown to be capable of matching the precision and accuracy of EPMA/WDS for major (concentration C> 0.1 mass fraction), minor (0.01= C= 0.1), and upper trace range (0.001< C< 0.01) constituents, even when significant peak interference occurs [2]. However, achieving the best analytical performance in practice with SEM/EDS or EPMA/WDS depends on measuring a properly prepared specimen that fulfills an often unstated requirement, namely that the only reason the measured x-ray intensities vary between the unknown and the standard (s) is that the composition is different. Geometric effects due to surface roughness can impact x-ray generation and propagation sufficiently to violate this basic requirement, resulting in relative error contributions of a factor as high as 10 in severe cases [3]. How smooth must a surface be to reduce such geometric effects to an acceptable level? In the early development of the k ratio protocol, Yakowitz interrupted the metallographic grinding and polishing procedure at various stages to examine the variance in the measured x-ray intensities due to surface roughness for pure gold (comparing AuMɑ vs. AuLɑ) and for a homogeneous brass alloy (comparing CuKɑ vs. ZnKɑ)[4]. That study revealed that polishing to the practical limit then achievable with available polishing compounds was necessary to reduce the variance contribution due to surface roughness to an acceptable level for the case of “soft” compared to “hard” radiation, eg, AuMɑ (2.12 keV) vs. AuLɑ,(9.71 keV). What level of surface roughness creates significant geometric effects for the much lower energy x-rays of light elements, such as OK= 0.523 keV? The NIST Monte Carlo simulation embedded in DTSA-II has been used to examine this question [5]. A crenellated surface was modeled with the spacing and depth parameters of the grooves as variables, as shown schematically in Figure 1 with the EDS detector oriented to look across the grooves. Figure 2 shows the k ratios for the low energy photons OK (0.523 keV) and FeL (0.704 keV) in FeO (wustite) as a function of the spacing and depth of crenellations, revealing that geometric effects persist at the level of 5% relative or greater down to crenellations with 100 nm height and lateral spacing. Polishing to a relief of less than 20 nm is needed to reduce the effects of surface roughness to a relative error contribution below 1% for these low energy photons.

This excerpt provides quantitative evidence primarily for standardless EDS accuracy and trace-element performance. Early standardless tests on known materials yielded a 95% relative-deviation range of ±25%, indicating substantially weaker accuracy than would generally be expected from a well-controlled standards-based k-ratio procedure; the excerpt does not provide a direct numerical standards-based k-ratio comparison. Standardless analysis needs beam energy and spectrometer takeoff angle, but not electron dose. Consequently, results—including assumed-stoichiometric oxygen—must be normalized to 100 wt%, unless dose information or peak-to-background methods recover a meaningful raw total. The authors estimate that standardless analysis produces perhaps 95% or more of EDS quantitative results and emphasize inadequate vendor documentation and testing. For trace constituents, NIST K523 at 20 keV used 26.6 million integrated counts; reported mass fractions include Mg 0.00097 with CDL 0.00019, P 0.0025 with CDL 0.00017, and other constituents near 0.002–0.006. It states that the k-ratio compares unknown and standard intensities, with k = Cstd(Iunk/Istd), and that the difference between k and the true mass fraction is corrected through matrix corrections. The corrections account for atomic-number effects (backscatter and electron energy loss), X-ray absorption, and secondary fluorescence. For EDS, the correction is a weighted combination of corrections for all transitions contributing to an integrated peak; this matters when lines lie on different sides of absorption edges or undergo self-absorption. Matrix-matched standards are preferred because [ZAF]unk/[ZAF]std is expected to be close to unity, allowing uncertainties in poorly known physical parameters to largely cancel. The excerpt warns that complex standards can have peak interferences. It recommends collecting approximately 5–10 standard spectra and multiple unknown acquisitions to identify outliers, test homogeneity, and reveal preparation or metrology problems. The REE example concerns minor/trace constituents below 10 wt%, with engineered glasses containing about 3–4 wt% REE, but no achieved accuracy, precision, or detection-limit values are given here.

The excerpt provides evidence for standards-based SEM-EDS quantification, but not for a direct numerical comparison with standardless accuracy. Spectra were collected using vendor software and processed with NIST DTSA-II; measured k-ratios were converted to concentration ratios using matrix corrections for electron retardation and backscattering, X-ray self-absorption, and secondary fluorescence, based on the Pouchou–Pichoir formulation. The study used certified, micrometer-homogeneous NIST standards, stoichiometric compounds for elements such as oxygen and sulfur, and other prepared microprobe standards. Abstract:

 Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDXS) in a transmission electron microscope is frequently used for the chemical analysis of Cu(In,Ga)Se2 (CIGS) solar cells with high spatial resolution. However, the quantification of EDXS data is complicated due to quantification errors and artifacts. This work shows how quantitative EDXS analyses of CIGS-based solar cells with Zn(O,S) buffer and ZnO-based window layers can be significantly improved. For this purpose, CIGS-based solar cells and a reference sample with a stack of Zn(O,S) layers with different [O]/[S] ratios were analyzed. We also show that a Pt-protection layer, deposited on the sample surface before FIB preparation of TEM lamellae, can induce artifacts that can be avoided by first depositing a carbon layer.

Abstract:
The partitioning behaviour of carbon, phosphorous and boron during the solidification of a resistance spot weld pool was studied using experimental simulations and a phase field model. Steels with varying carbon, phosphorous and boron contents were designed and subjected to a range of resistant spot welding thermal cycles. Mechanical properties were evaluated by hardness and cross tension tests and correlated with the weld microstructure. Phase field modelling results and experimental predictions show that the phosphorus concentration in the last area in the weld pool to solidify can reach about 0.38 wt% for a steel with a bulk concentration of 0.08 wt%. Elemental analysis indicates that in the absence of boron, the grain boundaries of columnar grains in the weld pool are decorated with phosphorous. As a result, a complete interface failure occurs during cross tension testing. With the addition of boron, apart from an increase in weld strength and plug diameter, the failure mode switches to a complete plug mode, resulting from the phosphorous depletion at the grain/inter-phase boundaries.

Additionally, the hardness and roughness of concrete surface under the coating layer (i.e., the interface between the coating and the surface) after four days of acid spraying, exhibited much smaller changes (due to protection) in contrast to the uncoated concrete specimens (used as blank/comparison experiments), which were found to be highly affected/corroded. The formation of concrete corrosion and coating by-products, as noticed after the respective chemical reactions, was recorded by X-ray diffraction (XRD) measurements and the respective quantification of obtained results. In all the coated specimens only very small amounts of the major by-product (gypsum) was observed, indicating that the concrete surface was sufficiently protected from sulfuric acid attack.

The paper characterizes SEM-EDS as suitable for routine quantitative analysis, while reserving EPMA-WDS for lower detection limits, difficult matrices, better spectral resolution, or finer spatial control. Thus, the excerpt supports general precision, sensitivity, and matrix-effect conclusions, but not the requested exact 0.4 wt% Mg results.

455

    Summary and prospects

           The analytical approach presented here demonstrates the viability of SEM-EDS analysis as a routine

      quantitative tool for volcanology and the geosciences more generally. The lower acquisition and upkeep costs and the

      simpler maintenance and operation of SEMs relative to EPMA has great potential to increase the accessibility of

460   quantitative in situ analysis. We do not, however, imagine that the SEM-EDS method presented here will completely

      supplant EPMA, instead we view it as a complementary technique whereby more routine analysis can be accomplished

     by SEM-EDS, reserving EPMA resources for applications that require lower detection limits, work on difficult

      matrices, enhanced spectral resolution, or more granular control of the spatial resolution offered by a field emission

      source microprobe. In addition to cost and simplicity advantages, SEM-EDS offers additional flexibility compared to

465  EPMA for the analysis of hydrous glasses. A range of area scans over a range of currents can quickly be acquired to

      demonstrate that the steps taken to mitigate Na mobility are successful on a sample-specific basis and the beam may

     be rastered over areas of varying geometry to accommodate squeezing spots onto constrained locations. Whereas the

      quality of “standardless” analysis has increased significantly, the acquisition of data suitable for publication

      nevertheless requires sourcing standards for method verification; accordingly, the marginal effort required for fully

### Artifact (ID artifact-00)

| Approach or performance aspect | Quantitative evidence | Interpretation for Mg in AlSi10Mg |

Detector window, matrix, contamination, oxidation, and background fitting must be validated for AlSi10Mg. |

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.
inventor.title: Inventor

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan for to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string representing the plan. It should be a dictionary
with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: open_targets_search
info.description:
Search for disease-target associations from OpenTargets database.

Adds new disease-target association data to the state and returns top search results.

List of disease names to search for.
Usage:
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Returns top targets for Alzheimer's
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's", "Diabetes"], target_names = ["PSEN1"] ->
    Filters for only PSEN1-Alzheimer's/Diabetes evidence
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"], drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: paper_search
info.description:
Search for papers in Google Scholar for you to look at.

Can be called repeatedly with identical parameters to retrieve more results (max 2 repeats).
A short summary of the retrieved papers will be returned, but to examine the full content of each paper,
you must use the gather_evidence tool.

query.description:
A Google Scholar search query, which can be a specific phrase, complete sentence,
or general keywords, e.g. 'machine learning for immunology'. Also can be
given search operators like 'author:'.
query.title: Query

min_year.description:
filter for minimum publication year.
The current year is 2026. If unsure about time range, do not set.
min_year.title: Min Year

max_year.description:
filter for maximum publication year.
The current year is 2026. If unsure about time range, do not set.
max_year.title: Max Year

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child
        - ADULT: Adult
        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting
        - SUSPENDED: Study suspended
        - TERMINATED: Study terminated
        - WITHDRAWN: Study withdrawn
        - AVAILABLE: Available
        - NO_LONGER_AVAILABLE: No longer available
        - TEMPORARILY_NOT_AVAILABLE: Temporarily not available
        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training
        - SUPPORTIVE_CARE: Supportive Care
        - SCREENING: Screening
        - HEALTH_SERVICES_RESEARCH: Health Services Research
        - BASIC_SCIENCE: Basic Science
        - DEVICE_FEASIBILITY: Device Feasibility
        - OTHER: Other

    InterventionType:
        - BEHAVIORAL: Behavioral interventions
        - BIOLOGICAL: Biological interventions
        - COMBINATION_PRODUCT: Combination product interventions
        - DEVICE: Device interventions
        - DIAGNOSTIC_TEST: Diagnostic test interventions
        - DIETARY_SUPPLEMENT: Dietary supplement interventions
        - DRUG: Drug interventions
        - GENETIC: Genetic interventions
        - PROCEDURE: Procedure interventions
        - RADIATION: Radiation interventions
        - OTHER: Other interventions

    DesignAllocation:
        - RANDOMIZED: Randomized allocation
        - NON_RANDOMIZED: Non-randomized allocation
        - NA: Not applicable

    InterventionalAssignment:

the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).

Abstract:
Abstract 2018 marked the 50th anniversary of the introduction of energy dispersive X-ray spectrometry (EDS) with semiconductor detectors to electron-excited X-ray microanalysis. Initially useful for qualitative analysis, EDS has developed into a fully quantitative analytical tool that can match wavelength dispersive spectrometry for accuracy in the determination of major (mass concentration C > 0.1) and minor (0.01 ≤ C ≤ 0.1) constituents, and useful accuracy can extend well into the trace (0.001 < C < 0.01) constituent range even when severe peak interference occurs. Accurate analysis is possible for low atomic number elements (B, C, N, O, and F), and at low beam energy, which can optimize lateral and depth spatial resolution. By recording a full EDS spectrum at each picture element of a scan, comprehensive quantitative compositional mapping can also be performed.

It is a great time to be a microanalyst. After a few decades of incremental progress in energy-dispersive X-ray spectrometry (EDS), the last decade has seen the accuracy and precision surge forward. Today, the question is not whether EDS is generally useful but to identify the types of problems for which wavelength-dispersive X-ray spectrometry remains the better choice. During AM fabrication, the melted feedstock material experiences fast thermal cycling due to the layer-by-layer deposition process resulting in microstructures and properties that are drastically different from the traditionally manufactured parts. For AM to become a viable process for fabricating critical components made of high-performance structural alloys, such as AlSi10Mg, a comprehensive understanding is required toward developing the process-structure-property relationships prevalent in AM. AlSi10Mg, with its good castability, strength, hardness, and dynamic properties, is typically used to fabricate structural components that are required to withstand high loads. This alloy has been consolidated predominantly by the laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) method and several critical mechanical properties, such as fatigue, have been reported to date. This article, first, summarizes the as-deposited and heat-treated microstructures of AlSi10Mg specimens fabricated by L-PBF. Then, the article discusses the linkages among the feedstock properties, printing parameters, specimen geometry, post-processing techniques, and fatigue properties. This discussion is followed by a section on the fatigue life prediction of AlSi10Mg specimens using computational modeling. Finally, the article identifies critical research gaps and pinpoints future research opportunities. Despite this progress, numerous processes and phenomena, along with the implications of producing components layer by layer on their performance under stress, remain inadequately explored. These factors not only affect microstructure but subsequently also the mechanical properties. The positioning of objects within the 3D printer’s workspace can thus significantly play a crucial role in their operational functionality, reliability, and safety of the equipment in an application. This article studies anisotropic properties and the influence of the printing orientation of aluminum alloy (AlSi10Mg) cylindrical tensile samples fabricated through an additive approach on their mechanical properties under tensile loading. Tensile testing of specimens covering seven different spatial orientations in the workspace of a 3D printing machine was performed according to ISO 6892-1 international standard. Minimum and maximum tensile properties (yield and ultimate tensile strength) have been observed in Y-sample and X-sample series, respectively. In contrast, elastic modulus of the 3D printed specimens was minimal for X-sample series, and maximal for Y-sample series. Fracture surfaces of the samples in seven basic spatial orientations were evaluated in synergy with the mechanical testing results determined by optical, electron microscopy, and electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) textural analysis to find correlation between the strength of the samples and the orientation of grains, their size and morphology. Furthermore, thermodynamic and Scheil–Gulliver simulation has been employed in order to explain the formation of intermetallic phases during additive manufacturing and further justifying observations in microstructure and mechanical properties. The disparity in texture intensity between these regions for samples Y(3) is likely responsible for localized mechanical incompatibilities and strain heterogeneity, resulting in preferential crack paths and reduced mechanical strength compared to the sample Z(3), which presented a more randomized orientation distribution with less distinguishable texture zones, enabling better strain accommodation and more uniform plastic deformation, which correlates with its higher tensile and yield strength. Nanoindentation has emerged as a key tool for probing these variations, yet systematic understanding of the links between processing parameters, microstructure, and nano-mechanical response remains limited. This critical review examines how laser processing parameters influence local mechanical response through their impact on microstructural features. Key challenges in interpreting nanoindentation are highlighted, alongside inconsistencies in experimental protocols and reporting practices that hinder cross-study comparisons. Beyond summarizing existing findings, underexplored aspects of nanoindentation in LPBF AlSi10Mg are identified, including spatially correlated microstructure-mechanical mapping, depth-resolved measurements, and integration with advanced characterization and data-driven approaches. By synthesizing current knowledge and clarifying methodological constraints, this review positions nanoindentation not merely as a descriptive tool, but as a mechanistically informed approach for linking processing conditions, microstructural heterogeneity, and local mechanical response. These insights aim to support more rigorous interpretation of small-scale mechanical data and to guide future studies toward predictive understanding and rational process optimization in additively manufactured aluminum alloys. Ultrahigh strength magnesium via solidification of nanocolloid Valid Text Names: 'nadendla2026ultrahighstrengthmagnesium pages 1-5', 'nadendla2026ultrahighstrengthmagnesium pages 5-10', 'nadendla2026ultrahighstrengthmagnesium pages 10-15', 'nadendla2026ultrahighstrengthmagnesium pages 15-18', 'nadendla2026ultrahighstrengthmagnesium pages 18-22', 'nadendla2026ultrahighstrengthmagnesium pages 22-25', 'nadendla2026ultrahighstrengthmagnesium pages 25-29', 'nadendla2026ultrahighstrengthmagnesium pages 29-34', 'nadendla2026ultrahighstrengthmagnesium pages 34-35' BibTex: @article{nadendla2026ultrahighstrengthmagnesium, author = "Nadendla, Hari Babu and Yang, Xinliang and Fang, Changming and Nishi, Shunsuke and Matsuda, Tomoki and Kambara, Makoto and Tanaka, Toshimi and Dougakiuchi, Masashi and Tang, Fengzai and West, Geoffrey and Wang, Shihao and Ramasse, Quentin", booktitle = "Nature Communications", journal = "Nature Communications", title = "Ultrahigh strength magnesium via solidification of nanocolloid", volume = "17", year = "2026", month = "Apr", doi = "10.1038/s41467-026-71671-x", url = "https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-71671-x" } Abstract: Abstract

We report a simple, scalable route to produce ultrahigh-strength magnesium (Mg) via solidification of a colloidal solution containing nanoscale niobium carbide (NbC) particles suspended in liquid magnesium (Mg(l)). A single-atom-level investigation reveals that NbC exhibits excellent spontaneous wetting with molten Mg, driven by the formation of an ordered layer of Mg atoms strongly bonded to the carbon atoms on the NbC {001} surface. This creates a novel type of Mg-coated NbC (Mg@NbC) particles in liquid Mg and is referred to as Mg(l)-Mg@NbC nanocolloid. This unique and spontaneous wetting behaviour enables uniform nanoparticle dispersion in the molten Mg without external fields, and in the solidified Mg matrix without the need for thermomechanical processing. The resulting NbC dispersoids act as coherent, hard reinforcement phases, significantly strengthening the Mg matrix. As a result, the Mg-NbC material exhibits ultrahigh tensile strength and stiffness, surpassing those of all previously reported Mg alloy systems.

Relevant Snippet:
The most rigorous quantitative electron-excited x-ray microanalysis that can be performed with scanning electron microscopy/energy dispersive x-ray spectrometry (SEM/EDS) follows the k ratio protocol: measure the x-ray intensity ratio k= Iunknown/Istandard for each element and calculate concentrations by applying matrix corrections for electron backscattering and energy loss (Z), x-ray absorption (A), and characteristic-and continuum-induced secondary x-ray fluorescence (F), as originally developed for the electron probe microanalyzer (EPMA) with wavelength dispersive spectrometry (WDS)[1]. By utilizing the k ratio protocol, SEM/EDS has been shown to be capable of matching the precision and accuracy of EPMA/WDS for major (concentration C> 0.1 mass fraction), minor (0.01= C= 0.1), and upper trace range (0.001< C< 0.01) constituents, even when significant peak interference occurs [2]. However, achieving the best analytical performance in practice with SEM/EDS or EPMA/WDS depends on measuring a properly prepared specimen that fulfills an often unstated requirement, namely that the only reason the measured x-ray intensities vary between the unknown and the standard (s) is that the composition is different. Geometric effects due to surface roughness can impact x-ray generation and propagation sufficiently to violate this basic requirement, resulting in relative error contributions of a factor as high as 10 in severe cases [3]. How smooth must a surface be to reduce such geometric effects to an acceptable level? In the early development of the k ratio protocol, Yakowitz interrupted the metallographic grinding and polishing procedure at various stages to examine the variance in the measured x-ray intensities due to surface roughness for pure gold (comparing AuMɑ vs. AuLɑ) and for a homogeneous brass alloy (comparing CuKɑ vs. ZnKɑ)[4]. That study revealed that polishing to the practical limit then achievable with available polishing compounds was necessary to reduce the variance contribution due to surface roughness to an acceptable level for the case of “soft” compared to “hard” radiation, eg, AuMɑ (2.12 keV) vs. AuLɑ,(9.71 keV). What level of surface roughness creates significant geometric effects for the much lower energy x-rays of light elements, such as OK= 0.523 keV? The NIST Monte Carlo simulation embedded in DTSA-II has been used to examine this question [5]. A crenellated surface was modeled with the spacing and depth parameters of the grooves as variables, as shown schematically in Figure 1 with the EDS detector oriented to look across the grooves. Figure 2 shows the k ratios for the low energy photons OK (0.523 keV) and FeL (0.704 keV) in FeO (wustite) as a function of the spacing and depth of crenellations, revealing that geometric effects persist at the level of 5% relative or greater down to crenellations with 100 nm height and lateral spacing. Polishing to a relief of less than 20 nm is needed to reduce the effects of surface roughness to a relative error contribution below 1% for these low energy photons.

Abstract:
With the purpose of recovering the metal values, in this study the copper slag was reduced by coke and biochar at 1250 °C in an argon gas atmosphere using the isothermal reduction/drop quenching technique. The phase compositions of metal, matte, and slag were determined using electron probe microanalysis (EPMA). The effects of reduction time and amount of reductant were investigated. The distribution of elements between metal/matte and slag was ascertained based on the elemental concentrations determined by EPMA. It was found that copper concentration in slag can be effectively decreased to approximately 0.4–0.6 wt% within 5 min by coke and biochar. Copper and nickel can also be successfully recovered into the copper alloy phase once settling has been accomplished.

Abstract:

 Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDXS) in a transmission electron microscope is frequently used for the chemical analysis of Cu(In,Ga)Se2 (CIGS) solar cells with high spatial resolution. However, the quantification of EDXS data is complicated due to quantification errors and artifacts. This work shows how quantitative EDXS analyses of CIGS-based solar cells with Zn(O,S) buffer and ZnO-based window layers can be significantly improved. For this purpose, CIGS-based solar cells and a reference sample with a stack of Zn(O,S) layers with different [O]/[S] ratios were analyzed. For Zn(O,S), the correction of sample-thickness-dependent absorption of low-energy O–Kα X-rays significantly improves the results of quantitative EDXS. Absorption of characteristic X-rays in CIGS is less relevant. However, for small transmission electron microscopy (TEM) sample thicknesses, artifacts can occur due to material changes by focused-ion-beam (FIB)-based preparation of TEM samples, electron-beam-induced damage, and oxidation of the sample surface. We also show that a Pt-protection layer, deposited on the sample surface before FIB preparation of TEM lamellae, can induce artifacts that can be avoided by first depositing a carbon layer.

Abstract:
The partitioning behaviour of carbon, phosphorous and boron during the solidification of a resistance spot weld pool was studied using experimental simulations and a phase field model. Steels with varying carbon, phosphorous and boron contents were designed and subjected to a range of resistant spot welding thermal cycles. Mechanical properties were evaluated by hardness and cross tension tests and correlated with the weld microstructure. Phase field modelling results and experimental predictions show that the phosphorus concentration in the last area in the weld pool to solidify can reach about 0.38 wt% for a steel with a bulk concentration of 0.08 wt%. Elemental analysis indicates that in the absence of boron, the grain boundaries of columnar grains in the weld pool are decorated with phosphorous. As a result, a complete interface failure occurs during cross tension testing. With the addition of boron, apart from an increase in weld strength and plug diameter, the failure mode switches to a complete plug mode, resulting from the phosphorous depletion at the grain/inter-phase boundaries.

Abstract:
Several coatings and linings have been examined and used for the protection of sewer concrete pipes, against mainly biogenic-provoked corrosion due to the production of bio-sulfuric acid, leading to the degradation of the pipes’ structure and eventually, to their collapse and need for costly replacement. This study aimed to examine the potential differences between five different magnesium hydroxide coatings, prepared from powders presenting different purity, surface area and pore size distribution, when applied as corrosion protection agents. These coatings were tested by using accelerated sulfuric acid spraying tests, both in dry and wet coating conditions. The coating adhesion ability and their microstructure were examined by the application of pull-off measurements and of SEM analysis, respectively and were found to present certain differences, regarding the adhesion ability and the surface morphologies. During the acid spraying procedure, the surface pH and the mass change of coated concrete specimens were recorded daily. The surface pH was reduced towards acidic values and the mass reduction approached almost −20% in comparison with the initial coating mass for certain cases. Additionally, the hardness and roughness of concrete surface under the coating layer (i.e., the interface between the coating and the surface) after four days of acid spraying, exhibited much smaller changes (due to protection) in contrast to the uncoated concrete specimens (used as blank/comparison experiments), which were found to be highly affected/corroded. The formation of concrete corrosion and coating by-products, as noticed after the respective chemical reactions, was recorded by X-ray diffraction (XRD) measurements and the respective quantification of obtained results. In all the coated specimens only very small amounts of the major by-product (gypsum) was observed, indicating that the concrete surface was sufficiently protected from sulfuric acid attack.

               <jats:p>Magnesium hydroxide was prepared under controlled conditions from aqueous Mg(NO3)2 and NaOH solutions. Functional polypropylene/Mg(OH)2 and polypropylene/polypropylene 1% maleic anhydride/Mg(OH)2 composites were prepared containing 10% or 30% Mg(OH)2. messages.content:
Most relevant evidence (with ids):

## pqac-00000012

From text 'andersenUnknownyearascanningelectron pages 15-17'.

NL Andersen and H Winslow. A scanning electron microscope-energy dispersive spectrometry (sem-eds) method for the quantitative analysis of common volcanic phases. Unknown journal, Unknown year.

The excerpt does not contain the exact 0.4 wt% Mg experiment requested: it does not identify the specific standards tested, their measured Mg values, numerical errors or bias, acquisition settings for that experiment, or explicit detection/reporting limits at 0.4 wt%. It does provide related information. Figure 5 states that Mg in olivine and pyroxene was evaluated using multiple calibration standards and that all Mg calibrations produced the same relative MgO trends. Differences in accuracy between standards were interpreted as evidence of matrix effects, although imperfect intercalibration could not be excluded. The broader method achieved detection limits of 0.04–0.08 wt% for Ca Kα1 and other lower-energy peaks, and 0.09–0.19 wt% for higher-energy peaks under the reported high-count conditions; relative standard deviation followed a negative power-law relationship with concentration down to 0.03 wt%. Increasing spectrum counts improved detection limits, but precision showed diminishing returns above approximately 1–1.5 million counts. The paper characterizes SEM-EDS as suitable for routine quantitative analysis, while reserving EPMA-WDS for lower detection limits, difficult matrices, better spectral resolution, or finer spatial control. Thus, the excerpt supports general precision, sensitivity, and matrix-effect conclusions, but not the requested exact 0.4 wt% Mg results.

It does indicate that calibration-standard-dependent accuracy differences were interpreted as matrix effects, although imperfect intercalibration could not be excluded. The method reports accuracy using relative percent difference (rpd) and precision using relative standard deviation (rsd). The supplied standards table includes low-Mg reference values near the requested concentration: San Carlos olivine has expected MgO of 0.37 wt% and Springwater olivine 0.30 wt%; fayalite is substantially higher at 2.14 wt%. For standardless analysis, 20 kV results were considered sufficiently accurate for research, but analytical totals were higher than ideal; using factory standards collected at a different voltage (15 kV) degraded accuracy and produced high totals. The excerpt gives glass-analysis acquisition examples at 15 kV and 3–3.2 nA with 0.25 × 10^6 counts over 6 s, but these are not identified as the 0.4 wt% Mg experiment. Overall glass data quality was said to be comparable to that of 26 electron-microprobe laboratories, while numerical method-wide minor/trace accuracy and precision values are absent here.
