      analysis (supplemental Table S3). Moreover, an accelerating voltage of 15 kV is often preferred for the analysis of

       silicate and oxide minerals as it provides a reasonable trade-off between the x-ray excitation of the elements of interest

     and the size of the x-ray generation volume (Shui-Yuan Yang et al., 2022)—the latter of which is a critical consideration

     when attempting analysis of finely zoned minerals, small inclusions, or vesiculated matrix glass.

300         Whereas standardless analysis in theory provides a simplified approach to quantitative analysis, acquiring

      geologically interpretable data requires performing the beam energy measurement and the analysis of secondary

       verification standards, and thus does not relieve the analyst of the effort of sourcing standards nor of using a large

     sample holder or sample exchanges to measure standards. The analysis of a full set of calibration standards typically

      requires less than one hour; accordingly, we find that the additional accuracy and flexibility of standardized analysis is

305  worth the relatively minor additional effort required.




     9     Long-term reproducibility of mineral standards

           The accuracy and precision of pyroxene, olivine, magnetite, ilmenite, and feldspar standards was evaluated

      using data acquired during multiple sessions from May 2023 to April 2025 (Fig. 7). The accuracy and precision of the

      standard results are comparable to typical EPMA methods as shown by the consistency of our standard results. For all

310  major elements except MnO, the rpd  is less than 5% and  is less than 2.5% for nearly  all standards (Fig. 7;

     Supplementary Table S5). MnO is present in major element levels in the SMS fayalite and SMS ilmenite standards

      (expected = 2.14 wt. % and 4.77 wt. %, respectively) and yields elevated rpd of 6.3% and 4.5%. In each case, the rsd

        is consistent with other analytes of similar concentrations indicating that heterogeneity of the standard is not likely the

      source of the inaccuracy. Standards with MnO concentrations < 1 wt. % yield accuracy consistent with other elements

315   of similar concentration. The MnO analyses of the fayalite and ilmenite standards were each calibrated using the other

     and therefore we conclude that the elevated rpd most likely reflect imperfect intercalibration of these two standards.

     The rpd of minor elements generally increases from approximately 5% to 30% for elements of concentration 1 to 0.1

      wt. %.

           The rsd of the major elements are mostly less than 2%, a handful are 2–5% for concentrations of 1–10 wt. %,

320  and are 3–30% for the minor elements. The rsd varies from approximately 3-5% for concentrations of 0.7–1 wt.% to

      approximately 30% for those of 0.15–0.2 wt. %. The rsd is strongly corelated with concentrations for all elements in

        all standards, with a slightly weaker correlation for the highest concentrations measured. In contrast, the rpd shows a

      general correlation with expected concentration but significantly more scatter. Neither the rpd nor rsd is correlated to

      the atomic number of the element.

325           In addition to the standard data reported here, analysis of unknown samples during this time period yielded

      consistently acceptable oxide  totals (100±2%  for nominally anhydrous phases without  substantial Fe3+) and

      stoichiometry (total formula cations ±0.03 of expected). Several unknown samples were measured by both EPMA-

   WDS and SEM-EDS or could be compared to published EPMA datasets; the SEM-EDS method produced results

      consistent with EPMA both for the concentrations of individual spots as well as derived parameters, for example, Fe-

330  Ti oxide temperatures and orthopyroxene Fe-Mg diffusion timescales (Andersen et al., 2025; Winslow et al., 2025).



     Analysis of beam-sensitive materials

           The migration of ions in beam-sensitive materials is a well-known difficulty with electron beam methods. This

       effect is particularly pronounced for the analysis of Na in hydrous volcanic glass (e.g., Iverson et al., 2017; Kuehn et

335   al., 2011). Beam damage may be mitigated by lowering the electron dose to the sample by increasing the analyzed

       area, decreasing the counting time, and/or lowering the beam current; however, Guyett et al. (2024) found that Na is

      mobilized by a beam current of only 300 pA during a one-minute analysis. EPMA methods may also implement a time-

      dependent intensity (TDI) correction to account for Na migration. TDI correction has not been implemented in any

      publicly available EDS software, so the Na migration must be mitigated by optimizing the electron dose.



     10340      We evaluated the mobility of Na and strategies for its mitigation in Na-rich feldspar and volcanic glass.

      Standards for these experiments are summarized in Table 1 and are from the SMS, the intercomparison study of Kuehn

       et al. (2011), the Panum crater obsidian of Jensen et al. (2021), which is equivalent material to standard OH-1 of Wu

       et al. (2022), and four samples from a yet unpublished interlaboratory comparison study (Britta Jensen, University of

      Alberta, 2023, personal communication). OIA does not have the capability to produce areas of a consistent, predefined

345  shape and aspect ratio in the “point and shoot” workflow. Rather, each area must be drawn by hand using a rectangle,

       ellipse, or freehand area tool. The dimensions of each rectangular and elliptical spot were confirmed using the feature

     measurement tool in the EDS software and the freehand areas were measured in exported images using image analysis

      software. The spot size for EPMA analysis is typically expressed as the beam diameter; we recast our spot sizes as the

      side length of a square of equivalent area, i.e., the square root of the raster area, so that the size of rasters with variable

350  aspect ratio can be directly compared in terms comparable to typical EPMA procedures. We measured approximate

      square and circles rasters of 1.2–59 µm and rectangles with aspect ratios up to 4.6:1.

        We initially tested if analyzing area rasters could mitigate Na mobility using our baseline mineral analytical

      setup. These analyses were performed at 15 kV, using a current of 2.5-3 nA, and collected 1.5x106 total counts,

      requiring an average analysis time of 63 s. Dead-times were 40–50% for spot analyses; analysis of area scans decreased

355   the count rate, yielding dead-times of approximately 30% for the same current.

           The Na-mobility behavior differed between two Na-rich feldspar standards, albite and anorthoclase. The albite

      standard yielded consistent Na2O concentrations for the point analysis and all rasters. In contrast the anorthoclase

     measurements displayed apparent Na-loss for the point analysis, but a raster of only a few µm was sufficient to mitigate

       this effect (Fig 8).

360         For the glass standards, the nominally anhydrous, subalkaline, and mafic VG-2 standard yielded consistent

     Na2O compositions for point analyses and all raster sizes, but all other glass standards displayed significant Na loss for

      the point and small raster analyses (Fig. 8). All standards but the Sheep Track tephra, discussed further below, produced

      consistent Na2O with a raster size of at least 10 µm, and the Na2O concentrations of some stabilized for spots as small

      as 5 µm. In addition to increasing the analysis area, decreasing the beam current may also mitigate Na mobility in glass.

365 We measured an additional set of points and rasters for a subset of the glass standards utilizing a current of 0.6–0.7 nA,

455

    Summary and prospects

           The analytical approach presented here demonstrates the viability of SEM-EDS analysis as a routine

      quantitative tool for volcanology and the geosciences more generally. The lower acquisition and upkeep costs and the

      simpler maintenance and operation of SEMs relative to EPMA has great potential to increase the accessibility of

460   quantitative in situ analysis. We do not, however, imagine that the SEM-EDS method presented here will completely

      supplant EPMA, instead we view it as a complementary technique whereby more routine analysis can be accomplished

     by SEM-EDS, reserving EPMA resources for applications that require lower detection limits, work on difficult

      matrices, enhanced spectral resolution, or more granular control of the spatial resolution offered by a field emission

      source microprobe. In addition to cost and simplicity advantages, SEM-EDS offers additional flexibility compared to

465  EPMA for the analysis of hydrous glasses. A range of area scans over a range of currents can quickly be acquired to

      demonstrate that the steps taken to mitigate Na mobility are successful on a sample-specific basis and the beam may

     be rastered over areas of varying geometry to accommodate squeezing spots onto constrained locations. Whereas the

      quality of “standardless” analysis has increased significantly, the acquisition of data suitable for publication

      nevertheless requires sourcing standards for method verification; accordingly, the marginal effort required for fully

470  standardized analysis is modest, with accompanying gains in accuracy and flexibility.

### Artifact (ID artifact-00)

| Approach or performance aspect | Quantitative evidence | Interpretation for Mg in AlSi10Mg |
|---|---|---|
| Matrix-matched, experimentally measured standard | For an exactly composition-matched standard, the unknown-to-standard matrix-correction ratio is 1.000; closely matched matrices keep it near unity. | Preferred when the certified value applies to the analyzed microscale volume. It minimizes dependence on absorption and atomic-number corrections. ICP-MS certifies bulk composition but does not prove micrometre-scale homogeneity. |
| Pure-element measured standards with ZAF or φ(ρz) correction | Experimental pure-element standards produced relative errors below 1% for major elements in a favorable alloy test; differences of 3–7% versus wet chemistry remained partly because of matrix corrections. These are general results, not AlSi10Mg-specific. | A rigorous and often excellent alternative. For Mg Kα in Al–Si, accuracy depends more strongly on the correction model, detector calibration, surface condition, and geometry than it does with a matrix-matched standard. |
| Vendor standardless quantification | Historical testing found that 95% of results were within approximately ±25% relative error. function.arguments:
{"answer": "# Quantifying 0.2–0.5 wt% Mg by SEM–EDS

## Bottom line

**Yes—provided it is homogeneous on the SEM interaction-volume scale, a well-characterized Al–Si–Mg matrix-matched standard is preferable for quantifying approximately 0.2–0.5 wt% Mg in AlSi10Mg.** Its advantage is not specifically that ICP-MS was used, but that it combines a traceable assigned Mg concentration with a matrix sufficiently similar to the unknown that the unknown/standard matrix-correction ratio approaches unity. Matrix matching therefore suppresses uncertainty from backscattering/stopping power, Mg Kα absorption, and secondary fluorescence. A perfectly composition-matched standard has a correction ratio of 1.000; near matching allows uncertain physical parameters to cancel substantially. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000002)

However, **bulk ICP-MS certification alone is insufficient**. ICP-MS establishes the bulk mean after dissolution, whereas SEM–EDS samples a micrometre-scale volume. An AlSi10Mg reference may contain α-Al, Si-rich regions, Mg-bearing precipitates, segregation, or porosity. It is suitable as a direct calibrant only if Mg and the effective matrix are homogeneous at the chosen interaction volume, or if enough large-area/random measurements reproduce the certified bulk mean. Otherwise, use measured pure-element or simple-compound standards for primary k-ratios and treat the ICP-MS-certified alloy as an independent quality-control material.

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

## What “matrix correction” and “matrix-correction error” mean

Standards-based analysis measures a k-ratio and applies a ZAF or φ(ρz) correction for atomic-number effects, X-ray absorption, and fluorescence. The **size of that correction is not itself the error**. Even a sizable correction can be accurate; error arises from uncertain correction parameters, inappropriate geometry, detector response, or a nonrepresentative standard. EDS corrections also combine all transitions fitted within a peak family, which can matter near absorption edges. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000005)

There is therefore no defensible universal statement such as “the Mg ZAF correction in AlSi10Mg is 10%.” It depends on beam voltage, take-off angle, line family, compositions, and correction implementation. The correct procedure is to export the Mg k-ratio and calculated correction factor for the actual method and validate the result against an independent Al–Si–Mg material.

As an illustration of scale—not an AlSi10Mg-specific result—an approximately 20% discrepancy between tabulated Mg Kα mass-absorption coefficients produced only about a 1% effect on calculated concentration in one EPMA example. This demonstrates why an uncertain physical coefficient cannot be equated directly with the concentration error. (pqac-00000005)

Experimental pure-element standards can nevertheless perform very well. In a favorable Fe–Cr–Ni alloy test, experimental standards reduced relative errors below 1% against NIST EDS values, although discrepancies of 3–7% remained relative to wet chemistry and were attributed partly to matrix correction. Low-energy/light-element analyses were substantially less robust in a chemically mismatched matrix. (pqac-00000006)

## Standardless error at 0.2–0.5 wt%

Historical testing of standardless EDS against known materials found that 95% of results occupied a broad **±25% relative-deviation range**. Standardless results also normally require normalization to 100% because electron dose is not measured; normalization can conceal missing elements and systematic intensity errors. Vendor algorithms and detector-efficiency calibrations vary and are often incompletely documented. (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000014)

Applied to 0.40 wt% Mg, ±25% relative corresponds to approximately **±0.10 wt% absolute**. Thus, standardless EDS may adequately establish “Mg is around 0.4 wt%,” but it should not be assumed capable of reliably distinguishing 0.35 from 0.45 wt% without local validation. This is a historical general-performance envelope, not a guaranteed error for every current system.

A recent standardized SEM–EDS study found that minor-element relative error generally increased from roughly 5% toward 30% as concentration decreased from 1 to 0.1 wt%; precision similarly deteriorated from about 3–5% RSD at 0.7–1 wt% to about 30% RSD at 0.15–0.2 wt%. Nearly all 0.1–1 wt% glass measurements were within 30% relative error. (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017)

Accordingly, realistic routine targets after method validation are approximately:

- **At 0.4–0.5 wt% Mg:** often about 5–15% relative, or roughly ±0.02–0.08 wt% absolute.
- **At 0.2 wt% Mg:** often about 10–30% relative, or roughly ±0.02–0.06 wt% absolute.
- **Best-case high-count, well-matched work:** potentially a few percent relative, but this must be demonstrated with replicate standards and independent controls rather than assumed.

These ranges are practical inferences from concentration-dependent data, not an AlSi10Mg-specific certified uncertainty budget.

## Detection limits and standards-based capability

For peaks without serious interference, modern standards-based EDS has achieved **0.02–0.05 wt% 3σ detection limits** with counting times below 500 s. In a 26.6-million-count NIST glass spectrum, Mg at 0.097 wt% had a critical detection limit of 0.019 wt%. (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015)

Under more routine conditions—15 kV, approximately 3 nA, and 1.5 million total counts—a recent study obtained detection limits of **0.04–0.08 wt% for lines at or below 3.69 keV** and 0.09–0.19 wt% for higher-energy lines. Mg Kα at approximately 1.25 keV belongs to the lower-energy category, although its actual limit in Al–Si must be measured. Increasing counts improved detection limits, but diminishing precision gains appeared above about 1–1.5 million total spectrum counts in that particular setup. (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018)

Thus 0.2–0.5 wt% Mg is normally **well above the EDS detection limit**. Detection is not the primary problem; accurate background subtraction, calibration, matrix correction, and representative sampling are. Detection limit also should not be confused with quantification limit: a 3σ detection may be statistically real while still having large relative uncertainty.

State-of-the-art EDS can accurately analyze the upper trace interval of 0.1–1 wt%, while WDS retains an advantage at the lowest concentrations because its spectral resolution gives a better peak-to-background ratio. (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000010)

## Recommended AlSi10Mg protocol

1. **Qualify the alloy standard.** Confirm its ICP-MS value and uncertainty, but also assess micrometre-scale Mg homogeneity by many points/rasters across multiple fields. Examine whether individual interaction volumes intersect Si particles or Mg-rich precipitates.
2. **Prefer co-mounting.** Polish unknown and standard together, or reproduce geometry, take-off angle, coating, working distance, beam voltage, current, and detector settings exactly. Surface roughness, oxide films, and contamination particularly affect low-energy Mg Kα photons. Conventional standards-based analyses generally show sensible raw totals of about 98–102%; inspect rather than automatically normalize anomalous totals. (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000007)
3. **Use true measured k-ratios.** Do not call a vendor’s remote factory library “standards-based” merely because standards generated that library. Measure the standard locally at the same beam energy and geometry.
4. **Retain pure/simple standards as a cross-check.** A strong design is local pure Al, Si, and Mg or suitable stable compounds for calibration, plus the ICP-MS-certified AlSi10Mg alloy as a secondary check. If both routes agree within the uncertainty target, confidence is substantially increased.
5. **Collect high-count replicate spectra.** Acquire approximately 5–10 measurements on each standard and multiple unknown fields; this identifies outliers and tests standard homogeneity. Counting statistics alone predict approximately 3.1%, 1%, 0.31%, and 0.1% precision for 10³, 10⁴, 10⁵, and 10⁶ net counts, respectively, but Mg net counts—not total spectrum counts—control Mg precision. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000005)
6. **Measure an empirical blank and LOD.** Use an Al–10Si material with negligible Mg, if available, and calculate the 3σ critical detection limit from the background beneath Mg Kα. Do not rely on a generic software LOD.
7. **Report uncertainty honestly.** Include standard-value uncertainty, replicate precision, between-field heterogeneity, blank/background uncertainty, correction-model validation, and beam-current stability. Report both unnormalized and normalized results and the raw total.
8. **Escalate when necessary.** If the required decision is tighter than approximately ±0.02–0.05 wt% Mg, or if microsegregation and peak/background limitations dominate, use EPMA-WDS or bulk ICP-OES/ICP-MS for the bulk alloy. SEM–EDS then remains valuable for spatial distributions rather than as the sole bulk-composition method.

## Conclusion

A demonstrably homogeneous, ICP-MS-value-assigned Al–Si–Mg standard is the preferred calibrant for 0.2–0.5 wt% Mg because matrix matching makes the correction ratio close to one. But **microhomogeneity and commutability are more important than the words “ICP-MS certified.”** Pure-element standards with validated ZAF/φ(ρz) correction remain rigorous and may be safer if the alloy reference is segregated. At 0.4 wt% Mg, unvalidated standardless analysis can plausibly incur errors near 0.1 wt% absolute, whereas optimized standards-based EDS should detect Mg readily and can often attain several-to-tens-of-percent relative accuracy, with approximately 0.02–0.08 wt% practical detection limits depending strongly on counts, matrix, and instrumentation."}

{"answer": "# Quantifying 0.2–0.5 wt% Mg by SEM–EDS

## Bottom line

Matrix matching therefore suppresses uncertainty from backscattering/stopping power, Mg Kα absorption, and secondary fluorescence. A perfectly composition-matched standard has a correction ratio of 1.000; near matching allows uncertain physical parameters to cancel substantially. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000002)

However, **bulk ICP-MS certification alone is insufficient**. ICP-MS establishes the bulk mean after dissolution, whereas SEM–EDS samples a micrometre-scale volume. An AlSi10Mg reference may contain α-Al, Si-rich regions, Mg-bearing precipitates, segregation, or porosity. It is suitable as a direct calibrant only if Mg and the effective matrix are homogeneous at the chosen interaction volume, or if enough large-area/random measurements reproduce the certified bulk mean. Otherwise, use measured pure-element or simple-compound standards for primary k-ratios and treat the ICP-MS-certified alloy as an independent quality-control material.

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

## What “matrix correction” and “matrix-correction error” mean

Standards-based analysis measures a k-ratio and applies a ZAF or φ(ρz) correction for atomic-number effects, X-ray absorption, and fluorescence. The **size of that correction is not itself the error**. Even a sizable correction can be accurate; error arises from uncertain correction parameters, inappropriate geometry, detector response, or a nonrepresentative standard. EDS corrections also combine all transitions fitted within a peak family, which can matter near absorption edges. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000005)

There is therefore no defensible universal statement such as “the Mg ZAF correction in AlSi10Mg is 10%.” It depends on beam voltage, take-off angle, line family, compositions, and correction implementation. The correct procedure is to export the Mg k-ratio and calculated correction factor for the actual method and validate the result against an independent Al–Si–Mg material.

As an illustration of scale—not an AlSi10Mg-specific result—an approximately 20% discrepancy between tabulated Mg Kα mass-absorption coefficients produced only about a 1% effect on calculated concentration in one EPMA example. This demonstrates why an uncertain physical coefficient cannot be equated directly with the concentration error. (pqac-00000005)

Experimental pure-element standards can nevertheless perform very well. In a favorable Fe–Cr–Ni alloy test, experimental standards reduced relative errors below 1% against NIST EDS values, although discrepancies of 3–7% remained relative to wet chemistry and were attributed partly to matrix correction. Low-energy/light-element analyses were substantially less robust in a chemically mismatched matrix. (pqac-00000006)

## Standardless error at 0.2–0.5 wt%

Historical testing of standardless EDS against known materials found that 95% of results occupied a broad **±25% relative-deviation range**. Standardless results also normally require normalization to 100% because electron dose is not measured; normalization can conceal missing elements and systematic intensity errors. Vendor algorithms and detector-efficiency calibrations vary and are often incompletely documented. (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000014)

Applied to 0.40 wt% Mg, ±25% relative corresponds to approximately **±0.10 wt% absolute**. Thus, standardless EDS may adequately establish “Mg is around 0.4 wt%,” but it should not be assumed capable of reliably distinguishing 0.35 from 0.45 wt% without local validation. This is a historical general-performance envelope, not a guaranteed error for every current system.

A recent standardized SEM–EDS study found that minor-element relative error generally increased from roughly 5% toward 30% as concentration decreased from 1 to 0.1 wt%; precision similarly deteriorated from about 3–5% RSD at 0.7–1 wt% to about 30% RSD at 0.15–0.2 wt%. Nearly all 0.1–1 wt% glass measurements were within 30% relative error. (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017)

Accordingly, realistic routine targets after method validation are approximately:

- **At 0.4–0.5 wt% Mg:** often about 5–15% relative, or roughly ±0.02–0.08 wt% absolute.
- **At 0.2 wt% Mg:** often about 10–30% relative, or roughly ±0.02–0.06 wt% absolute.
- **Best-case high-count, well-matched work:** potentially a few percent relative, but this must be demonstrated with replicate standards and independent controls rather than assumed.

These ranges are practical inferences from concentration-dependent data, not an AlSi10Mg-specific certified uncertainty budget.

## Detection limits and standards-based capability

For peaks without serious interference, modern standards-based EDS has achieved **0.02–0.05 wt% 3σ detection limits** with counting times below 500 s. In a 26.6-million-count NIST glass spectrum, Mg at 0.097 wt% had a critical detection limit of 0.019 wt%. (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015)

Mg Kα at approximately 1.25 keV belongs to the lower-energy category, although its actual limit in Al–Si must be measured. Increasing counts improved detection limits, but diminishing precision gains appeared above about 1–1.5 million total spectrum counts in that particular setup. (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018)

Thus 0.2–0.5 wt% Mg is normally **well above the EDS detection limit**. Detection is not the primary problem; accurate background subtraction, calibration, matrix correction, and representative sampling are. Detection limit also should not be confused with quantification limit: a 3σ detection may be statistically real while still having large relative uncertainty.

State-of-the-art EDS can accurately analyze the upper trace interval of 0.1–1 wt%, while WDS retains an advantage at the lowest concentrations because its spectral resolution gives a better peak-to-background ratio. (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000010)

1. **Qualify the alloy standard.** Confirm its ICP-MS value and uncertainty, but also assess micrometre-scale Mg homogeneity by many points/rasters across multiple fields. Examine whether individual interaction volumes intersect Si particles or Mg-rich precipitates.

This demonstrates why an uncertain physical coefficient cannot be equated directly with the concentration error. (pqac-00000005)

Experimental pure-element standards can nevertheless perform very well. In a favorable Fe–Cr–Ni alloy test, experimental standards reduced relative errors below 1% against NIST EDS values, although discrepancies of 3–7% remained relative to wet chemistry and were attributed partly to matrix correction. Low-energy/light-element analyses were substantially less robust in a chemically mismatched matrix. (pqac-00000006)

## Standardless error at 0.2–0.5 wt%

Historical testing of standardless EDS against known materials found that 95% of results occupied a broad **±25% relative-deviation range**. Standardless results also normally require normalization to 100% because electron dose is not measured; normalization can conceal missing elements and systematic intensity errors. Vendor algorithms and detector-efficiency calibrations vary and are often incompletely documented. (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000014)

Applied to 0.40 wt% Mg, ±25% relative corresponds to approximately **±0.10 wt% absolute**. Thus, standardless EDS may adequately establish “Mg is around 0.4 wt%,” but it should not be assumed capable of reliably distinguishing 0.35 from 0.45 wt% without local validation. This is a historical general-performance envelope, not a guaranteed error for every current system.

A recent standardized SEM–EDS study found that minor-element relative error generally increased from roughly 5% toward 30% as concentration decreased from 1 to 0.1 wt%; precision similarly deteriorated from about 3–5% RSD at 0.7–1 wt% to about 30% RSD at 0.15–0.2 wt%. Nearly all 0.1–1 wt% glass measurements were within 30% relative error. (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017)

Accordingly, realistic routine targets after method validation are approximately:

- **At 0.4–0.5 wt% Mg:** often about 5–15% relative, or roughly ±0.02–0.08 wt% absolute.
- **At 0.2 wt% Mg:** often about 10–30% relative, or roughly ±0.02–0.06 wt% absolute.
- **Best-case high-count, well-matched work:** potentially a few percent relative, but this must be demonstrated with replicate standards and independent controls rather than assumed.

These ranges are practical inferences from concentration-dependent data, not an AlSi10Mg-specific certified uncertainty budget.

## Detection limits and standards-based capability

For peaks without serious interference, modern standards-based EDS has achieved **0.02–0.05 wt% 3σ detection limits** with counting times below 500 s. In a 26.6-million-count NIST glass spectrum, Mg at 0.097 wt% had a critical detection limit of 0.019 wt%. (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015)

Under more routine conditions—15 kV, approximately 3 nA, and 1.5 million total counts—a recent study obtained detection limits of **0.04–0.08 wt% for lines at or below 3.69 keV** and 0.09–0.19 wt% for higher-energy lines. Mg Kα at approximately 1.25 keV belongs to the lower-energy category, although its actual limit in Al–Si must be measured. Increasing counts improved detection limits, but diminishing precision gains appeared above about 1–1.5 million total spectrum counts in that particular setup. (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018)

Thus 0.2–0.5 wt% Mg is normally **well above the EDS detection limit**. Detection is not the primary problem; accurate background subtraction, calibration, matrix correction, and representative sampling are. Detection limit also should not be confused with quantification limit: a 3σ detection may be statistically real while still having large relative uncertainty.

State-of-the-art EDS can accurately analyze the upper trace interval of 0.1–1 wt%, while WDS retains an advantage at the lowest concentrations because its spectral resolution gives a better peak-to-background ratio. (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000010)

## Recommended AlSi10Mg protocol

1. **Qualify the alloy standard.** Confirm its ICP-MS value and uncertainty, but also assess micrometre-scale Mg homogeneity by many points/rasters across multiple fields. Examine whether individual interaction volumes intersect Si particles or Mg-rich precipitates.
2. **Prefer co-mounting.** Polish unknown and standard together, or reproduce geometry, take-off angle, coating, working distance, beam voltage, current, and detector settings exactly. Surface roughness, oxide films, and contamination particularly affect low-energy Mg Kα photons. Conventional standards-based analyses generally show sensible raw totals of about 98–102%; inspect rather than automatically normalize anomalous totals. (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000007)
3. **Use true measured k-ratios.** Do not call a vendor’s remote factory library “standards-based” merely because standards generated that library. Measure the standard locally at the same beam energy and geometry.
4. **Retain pure/simple standards as a cross-check.** A strong design is local pure Al, Si, and Mg or suitable stable compounds for calibration, plus the ICP-MS-certified AlSi10Mg alloy as a secondary check. If both routes agree within the uncertainty target, confidence is substantially increased.
5. **Collect high-count replicate spectra.** Acquire approximately 5–10 measurements on each standard and multiple unknown fields; this identifies outliers and tests standard homogeneity. Counting statistics alone predict approximately 3.1%, 1%, 0.31%, and 0.1% precision for 10³, 10⁴, 10⁵, and 10⁶ net counts, respectively, but Mg net counts—not total spectrum counts—control Mg precision. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000005)
6. **Measure an empirical blank and LOD.** Use an Al–10Si material with negligible Mg, if available, and calculate the 3σ critical detection limit from the background beneath Mg Kα. Do not rely on a generic software LOD.
7. **Report uncertainty honestly.** Include standard-value uncertainty, replicate precision, between-field heterogeneity, blank/background uncertainty, correction-model validation, and beam-current stability. Report both unnormalized and normalized results and the raw total.
8. **Escalate when necessary.** If the required decision is tighter than approximately ±0.02–0.05 wt% Mg, or if microsegregation and peak/background limitations dominate, use EPMA-WDS or bulk ICP-OES/ICP-MS for the bulk alloy. SEM–EDS then remains valuable for spatial distributions rather than as the sole bulk-composition method.

## Conclusion

A demonstrably homogeneous, ICP-MS-value-assigned Al–Si–Mg standard is the preferred calibrant for 0.2–0.5 wt% Mg because matrix matching makes the correction ratio close to one. But **microhomogeneity and commutability are more important than the words “ICP-MS certified.”** Pure-element standards with validated ZAF/φ(ρz) correction remain rigorous and may be safer if the alloy reference is segregated. At 0.4 wt% Mg, unvalidated standardless analysis can plausibly incur errors near 0.1 wt% absolute, whereas optimized standards-based EDS should detect Mg readily and can often attain several-to-tens-of-percent relative accuracy, with approximately 0.02–0.08 wt% practical detection limits depending strongly on counts, matrix, and instrumentation.

It states that the k-ratio compares unknown and standard intensities, with k = Cstd(Iunk/Istd), and that the difference between k and the true mass fraction is corrected through matrix corrections. The corrections account for atomic-number effects (backscatter and electron energy loss), X-ray absorption, and secondary fluorescence. For EDS, the correction is a weighted combination of corrections for all transitions contributing to an integrated peak; this matters when lines lie on different sides of absorption edges or undergo self-absorption. Matrix-matched standards are preferred because [ZAF]unk/[ZAF]std is expected to be close to unity, allowing uncertainties in poorly known physical parameters to largely cancel. The excerpt warns that complex standards can have peak interferences. It recommends collecting approximately 5–10 standard spectra and multiple unknown acquisitions to identify outliers, test homogeneity, and reveal preparation or metrology problems. The REE example concerns minor/trace constituents below 10 wt%, with engineered glasses containing about 3–4 wt% REE, but no achieved accuracy, precision, or detection-limit values are given here.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides qualitative and formula-level evidence relevant to quantitative SEM-EDS/EPMA measurement, but it does not supply the requested numerical comparisons of standards-based versus standardless accuracy, numerical ZAF factors, errors at 0.2–0.5 wt%, precision, or detection limits. Castaing’s standards-based approach uses the ratio of characteristic X-ray intensities from an unknown and a standard, intended to eliminate spectrometer-efficiency calibration effects and relate the ratio to composition. Quantification requires matrix corrections for atomic-number effects (Z), X-ray absorption (A), and fluorescence (F), expressed as k_i = c_i Z_i A_i F_i. Absorption is identified as often the largest correction, especially for long-wavelength, low-energy X-rays; key parameters include beam energy, takeoff angle, and mass absorption coefficients. The excerpt warns that poorly characterized standards can produce the largest errors and recommends pure-element or stoichiometric oxide standards when possible. Spectral overlaps remain a major quantitative pitfall: examples include V Kα/Ti Kβ, B Kα/Mo M lines, and unresolved Pb Lα–As Kα and Pb Mα–S Kα peaks. contexts.context: The excerpt provides quantitative evidence mainly about matrix corrections and measurement pitfalls, not about standardless-vs-standards accuracy, 0.2–0.5 wt% errors, formal detection limits, or peak-interference statistics. For a homogeneous 50:50 Cu–Al alloy analyzed at 15 kV and a 52.5° takeoff angle, the Cu and Al elemental k-ratios are 0.45732 and 0.34037, while the corresponding ZAF corrections are 1.0933 and 1.4690. The Al correction is explicitly described as 47%, substantially above the pure-element correction of 1.0. Applying a homogeneous-alloy correction when the beam straddles distinct phases can overcorrect both x-ray intensities because matrix corrections are nonlinear; this can produce an artificially high total. Features smaller than the electron beam cannot be reliably interpreted compositionally, whereas very fine phases below about 0.05 microns may average out, yielding only an average composition. Preparation and geometry are critical: rough surfaces can bias analyses against low-energy x-rays, incorrect tilt can block detector line-of-sight, and coating composition/thickness must match between standards and unknowns. Carbon-coat transmission falls markedly for light-element lines: at 40 nm carbon, transmission is 93.355% for F Kα, 87.484% for O Kα, and 75.935% for N Kα.

answer.formatted_answer:
Question: For quantifying a minor element at 0.2-0.5 wt% (e.g. Mg in an Al-10Si-0.4Mg alloy, AlSi10Mg) by SEM-EDS, is a matrix-matched standard whose bulk composition was certified by ICP-MS preferable to pure-element standards? How large are matrix (ZAF) correction and standardless-quantification errors at such concentrations, and what accuracy and detection limits can standards-based EDS achieve for minor/trace elements?

# Quantifying 0.2–0.5 wt% Mg by SEM–EDS

## Bottom line

**Yes—provided it is homogeneous on the SEM interaction-volume scale, a well-characterized Al–Si–Mg matrix-matched standard is preferable for quantifying approximately 0.2–0.5 wt% Mg in AlSi10Mg.** Its advantage is not specifically that ICP-MS was used, but that it combines a traceable assigned Mg concentration with a matrix sufficiently similar to the unknown that the unknown/standard matrix-correction ratio approaches unity. Matrix matching therefore suppresses uncertainty from backscattering/stopping power, Mg Kα absorption, and secondary fluorescence. A perfectly composition-matched standard has a correction ratio of 1.000; near matching allows uncertain physical parameters to cancel substantially. (ritchie2018exploringthelimits pages 4-5, donovan2014electronprobemicroanalysis pages 23-26)

However, **bulk ICP-MS certification alone is insufficient**. ICP-MS establishes the bulk mean after dissolution, whereas SEM–EDS samples a micrometre-scale volume. An AlSi10Mg reference may contain α-Al, Si-rich regions, Mg-bearing precipitates, segregation, or porosity. It is suitable as a direct calibrant only if Mg and the effective matrix are homogeneous at the chosen interaction volume, or if enough large-area/random measurements reproduce the certified bulk mean. Otherwise, use measured pure-element or simple-compound standards for primary k-ratios and treat the ICP-MS-certified alloy as an independent quality-control material.

| Approach or performance aspect | Quantitative evidence | Interpretation for Mg in AlSi10Mg |
|---|---|---|
| Matrix-matched, experimentally measured standard | For an exactly composition-matched standard, the unknown-to-standard matrix-correction ratio is 1.000; closely matched matrices keep it near unity. | Preferred when the certified value applies to the analyzed microscale volume. It minimizes dependence on absorption and atomic-number corrections. ICP-MS certifies bulk composition but does not prove micrometre-scale homogeneity. |
| Pure-element measured standards with ZAF or φ(ρz) correction | Experimental pure-element standards produced relative errors below 1% for major elements in a favorable alloy test; differences of 3–7% versus wet chemistry remained partly because of matrix corrections. These are general results, not AlSi10Mg-specific. | A rigorous and often excellent alternative. For Mg Kα in Al–Si, accuracy depends more strongly on the correction model, detector calibration, surface condition, and geometry than it does with a matrix-matched standard. |
| Vendor standardless quantification | Historical testing found that 95% of results were within approximately ±25% relative error. Performance varies with vendor, software version, energy calibration, and detector-efficiency model. This is a general literature result. | At 0.40 wt% Mg, ±25% relative equals approximately ±0.10 wt% absolute. It is useful for screening but not reliably for distinguishing 0.35 from 0.45 wt%. |
| Practical standards-based detection limit at about 1.5 million counts | At 15 kV and approximately 3 nA, reported 3σ limits were 0.04–0.08 wt% for lines at or below 3.69 keV and 0.09–0.19 wt% for higher-energy lines. This was a general silicate and oxide study. | Mg Kα at 1.25 keV belongs to the favorable low-energy group. Mg at 0.2–0.5 wt% should be detectable, although quantification uncertainty may remain much larger than the detection limit. |
| High-count standards-based detection limit | Without severe overlap, reported 3σ limits were 0.02–0.05 wt% with counting times below 500 s. In a 26.6-million-count glass spectrum, 0.097 wt% Mg had a critical detection limit of 0.019 wt%. These are general glass results. | Mg below 0.1 wt% can be detected under optimized conditions. Detector window, matrix, contamination, oxidation, and background fitting must be validated for AlSi10Mg. |
| Expected accuracy and precision near 0.2–0.5 wt% | In a standardized SEM-EDS method, relative error generally increased from about 5% at 1 wt% toward 30% at 0.1 wt%; RSD was about 30% at 0.15–0.2 wt% and improved with concentration. These are general mineral and glass results. | A reasonable routine expectation after validation is about 10–30% relative uncertainty near 0.2 wt% and potentially 5–15% near 0.4–0.5 wt%, not an automatic guarantee. At 0.40 wt%, that is approximately ±0.02–0.12 wt% absolute. |
| Matrix-correction magnitude versus correction uncertainty | ZAF corrections can be appreciable, but their magnitude is composition- and voltage-specific. In one general example, an approximately 20% difference in a Mg Kα mass-absorption coefficient changed calculated concentration by only about 1%. | There is no universal Mg ZAF error. Calculate the actual correction ratio for the chosen standards and conditions, then validate it with an independent Al–Si–Mg reference material. |


*Table: Comparison of calibration approaches and realistic performance near 0.2–0.5 wt% Mg. Values are general literature benchmarks unless explicitly interpreted for AlSi10Mg.*

## What “matrix correction” and “matrix-correction error” mean

Standards-based analysis measures a k-ratio and applies a ZAF or φ(ρz) correction for atomic-number effects, X-ray absorption, and fluorescence. The **size of that correction is not itself the error**. Even a sizable correction can be accurate; error arises from uncertain correction parameters, inappropriate geometry, detector response, or a nonrepresentative standard. EDS corrections also combine all transitions fitted within a peak family, which can matter near absorption edges. (ritchie2018exploringthelimits pages 4-5, donovan2014electronprobemicroanalysis pages 20-23)

There is therefore no defensible universal statement such as “the Mg ZAF correction in AlSi10Mg is 10%.” It depends on beam voltage, take-off angle, line family, compositions, and correction implementation. The correct procedure is to export the Mg k-ratio and calculated correction factor for the actual method and validate the result against an independent Al–Si–Mg material.

As an illustration of scale—not an AlSi10Mg-specific result—an approximately 20% discrepancy between tabulated Mg Kα mass-absorption coefficients produced only about a 1% effect on calculated concentration in one EPMA example. This demonstrates why an uncertain physical coefficient cannot be equated directly with the concentration error. (donovan2014electronprobemicroanalysis pages 20-23)

Experimental pure-element standards can nevertheless perform very well. In a favorable Fe–Cr–Ni alloy test, experimental standards reduced relative errors below 1% against NIST EDS values, although discrepancies of 3–7% remained relative to wet chemistry and were attributed partly to matrix correction. Low-energy/light-element analyses were substantially less robust in a chemically mismatched matrix. (tong2026measurementuncertaintiesof pages 21-24)

## Standardless error at 0.2–0.5 wt%

Historical testing of standardless EDS against known materials found that 95% of results occupied a broad **±25% relative-deviation range**. Standardless results also normally require normalization to 100% because electron dose is not measured; normalization can conceal missing elements and systematic intensity errors. Vendor algorithms and detector-efficiency calibrations vary and are often incompletely documented. (newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 18-20)

Applied to 0.40 wt% Mg, ±25% relative corresponds to approximately **±0.10 wt% absolute**. Thus, standardless EDS may adequately establish “Mg is around 0.4 wt%,” but it should not be assumed capable of reliably distinguishing 0.35 from 0.45 wt% without local validation. This is a historical general-performance envelope, not a guaranteed error for every current system.

A recent standardized SEM–EDS study found that minor-element relative error generally increased from roughly 5% toward 30% as concentration decreased from 1 to 0.1 wt%; precision similarly deteriorated from about 3–5% RSD at 0.7–1 wt% to about 30% RSD at 0.15–0.2 wt%. Nearly all 0.1–1 wt% glass measurements were within 30% relative error. (andersenUnknownyearascanningelectron pages 10-12, andersenUnknownyearascanningelectron pages 12-15)

Accordingly, realistic routine targets after method validation are approximately:

- **At 0.4–0.5 wt% Mg:** often about 5–15% relative, or roughly ±0.02–0.08 wt% absolute.
- **At 0.2 wt% Mg:** often about 10–30% relative, or roughly ±0.02–0.06 wt% absolute.
- **Best-case high-count, well-matched work:** potentially a few percent relative, but this must be demonstrated with replicate standards and independent controls rather than assumed.

These ranges are practical inferences from concentration-dependent data, not an AlSi10Mg-specific certified uncertainty budget.

## Detection limits and standards-based capability

For peaks without serious interference, modern standards-based EDS has achieved **0.02–0.05 wt% 3σ detection limits** with counting times below 500 s. In a 26.6-million-count NIST glass spectrum, Mg at 0.097 wt% had a critical detection limit of 0.019 wt%. (newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 13-15, newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 18-20)

Under more routine conditions—15 kV, approximately 3 nA, and 1.5 million total counts—a recent study obtained detection limits of **0.04–0.08 wt% for lines at or below 3.69 keV** and 0.09–0.19 wt% for higher-energy lines. Mg Kα at approximately 1.25 keV belongs to the lower-energy category, although its actual limit in Al–Si must be measured. Increasing counts improved detection limits, but diminishing precision gains appeared above about 1–1.5 million total spectrum counts in that particular setup. (andersenUnknownyearascanningelectron pages 12-15, andersenUnknownyearascanningelectron pages 15-17)

Thus 0.2–0.5 wt% Mg is normally **well above the EDS detection limit**. Detection is not the primary problem; accurate background subtraction, calibration, matrix correction, and representative sampling are. Detection limit also should not be confused with quantification limit: a 3σ detection may be statistically real while still having large relative uncertainty.

State-of-the-art EDS can accurately analyze the upper trace interval of 0.1–1 wt%, while WDS retains an advantage at the lowest concentrations because its spectral resolution gives a better peak-to-background ratio. (ritchie2018exploringthelimits pages 1-4)

## Recommended AlSi10Mg protocol

1. **Qualify the alloy standard.** Confirm its ICP-MS value and uncertainty, but also assess micrometre-scale Mg homogeneity by many points/rasters across multiple fields. Examine whether individual interaction volumes intersect Si particles or Mg-rich precipitates.
2. **Prefer co-mounting.** Polish unknown and standard together, or reproduce geometry, take-off angle, coating, working distance, beam voltage, current, and detector settings exactly. Surface roughness, oxide films, and contamination particularly affect low-energy Mg Kα photons. Conventional standards-based analyses generally show sensible raw totals of about 98–102%; inspect rather than automatically normalize anomalous totals. (newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 3-4, tong2026measurementuncertaintiesof pages 8-11)
3. **Use true measured k-ratios.** Do not call a vendor’s remote factory library “standards-based” merely because standards generated that library. Measure the standard locally at the same beam energy and geometry.
4. **Retain pure/simple standards as a cross-check.** A strong design is local pure Al, Si, and Mg or suitable stable compounds for calibration, plus the ICP-MS-certified AlSi10Mg alloy as a secondary check. If both routes agree within the uncertainty target, confidence is substantially increased.
5. **Collect high-count replicate spectra.** Acquire approximately 5–10 measurements on each standard and multiple unknown fields; this identifies outliers and tests standard homogeneity. Counting statistics alone predict approximately 3.1%, 1%, 0.31%, and 0.1% precision for 10³, 10⁴, 10⁵, and 10⁶ net counts, respectively, but Mg net counts—not total spectrum counts—control Mg precision. (ritchie2018exploringthelimits pages 4-5, donovan2014electronprobemicroanalysis pages 20-23)
6. **Measure an empirical blank and LOD.** Use an Al–10Si material with negligible Mg, if available, and calculate the 3σ critical detection limit from the background beneath Mg Kα. Do not rely on a generic software LOD.
7. **Report uncertainty honestly.** Include standard-value uncertainty, replicate precision, between-field heterogeneity, blank/background uncertainty, correction-model validation, and beam-current stability. Report both unnormalized and normalized results and the raw total.
8. **Escalate when necessary.** If the required decision is tighter than approximately ±0.02–0.05 wt% Mg, or if microsegregation and peak/background limitations dominate, use EPMA-WDS or bulk ICP-OES/ICP-MS for the bulk alloy. SEM–EDS then remains valuable for spatial distributions rather than as the sole bulk-composition method.

## Conclusion

A demonstrably homogeneous, ICP-MS-value-assigned Al–Si–Mg standard is the preferred calibrant for 0.2–0.5 wt% Mg because matrix matching makes the correction ratio close to one. But **microhomogeneity and commutability are more important than the words “ICP-MS certified.”** Pure-element standards with validated ZAF/φ(ρz) correction remain rigorous and may be safer if the alloy reference is segregated. At 0.4 wt% Mg, unvalidated standardless analysis can plausibly incur errors near 0.1 wt% absolute, whereas optimized standards-based EDS should detect Mg readily and can often attain several-to-tens-of-percent relative accuracy, with approximately 0.02–0.08 wt% practical detection limits depending strongly on counts, matrix, and instrumentation.

| Approach or performance aspect | Quantitative evidence | Interpretation for Mg in AlSi10Mg |
|---|---|---|
| Matrix-matched, experimentally measured standard | For an exactly composition-matched standard, the unknown-to-standard matrix-correction ratio is 1.000; closely matched matrices keep it near unity. | Preferred when the certified value applies to the analyzed microscale volume. It minimizes dependence on absorption and atomic-number corrections. ICP-MS certifies bulk composition but does not prove micrometre-scale homogeneity. |
| Pure-element measured standards with ZAF or φ(ρz) correction | Experimental pure-element standards produced relative errors below 1% for major elements in a favorable alloy test; differences of 3–7% versus wet chemistry remained partly because of matrix corrections. These are general results, not AlSi10Mg-specific. | A rigorous and often excellent alternative. For Mg Kα in Al–Si, accuracy depends more strongly on the correction model, detector calibration, surface condition, and geometry than it does with a matrix-matched standard. |
| Vendor standardless quantification | Historical testing found that 95% of results were within approximately ±25% relative error. Performance varies with vendor, software version, energy calibration, and detector-efficiency model. This is a general literature result. | At 0.40 wt% Mg, ±25% relative equals approximately ±0.10 wt% absolute. It is useful for screening but not reliably for distinguishing 0.35 from 0.45 wt%. |
| Practical standards-based detection limit at about 1.5 million counts | At 15 kV and approximately 3 nA, reported 3σ limits were 0.04–0.08 wt% for lines at or below 3.69 keV and 0.09–0.19 wt% for higher-energy lines. This was a general silicate and oxide study. | Mg Kα at 1.25 keV belongs to the favorable low-energy group. Mg at 0.2–0.5 wt% should be detectable, although quantification uncertainty may remain much larger than the detection limit. |
| High-count standards-based detection limit | Without severe overlap, reported 3σ limits were 0.02–0.05 wt% with counting times below 500 s. In a 26.6-million-count glass spectrum, 0.097 wt% Mg had a critical detection limit of 0.019 wt%. These are general glass results. | Mg below 0.1 wt% can be detected under optimized conditions. Detector window, matrix, contamination, oxidation, and background fitting must be validated for AlSi10Mg. |
| Expected accuracy and precision near 0.2–0.5 wt% | In a standardized SEM-EDS method, relative error generally increased from about 5% at 1 wt% toward 30% at 0.1 wt%; RSD was about 30% at 0.15–0.2 wt% and improved with concentration. These are general mineral and glass results. | A reasonable routine expectation after validation is about 10–30% relative uncertainty near 0.2 wt% and potentially 5–15% near 0.4–0.5 wt%, not an automatic guarantee. At 0.40 wt%, that is approximately ±0.02–0.12 wt% absolute. |
| Matrix-correction magnitude versus correction uncertainty | ZAF corrections can be appreciable, but their magnitude is composition- and voltage-specific. In one general example, an approximately 20% difference in a Mg Kα mass-absorption coefficient changed calculated concentration by only about 1%. | There is no universal Mg ZAF error. Calculate the actual correction ratio for the chosen standards and conditions, then validate it with an independent Al–Si–Mg reference material. |

info.query: For quantifying a minor element at 0.2-0.5 wt% (e.g. Mg in an Al-10Si-0.4Mg alloy, AlSi10Mg) by SEM-EDS, is a matrix-matched standard whose bulk composition was certified by ICP-MS preferable to pure-element standards? How large are matrix (ZAF) correction and standardless-quantification errors at such concentrations, and what accuracy and detection limits can standards-based EDS achieve for minor/trace elements?
